analysis.one_liner: Tightens the rules on companies that treat employees as independent contractors to avoid payroll taxes and benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by a Democrat with two Republican cosponsors, was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on February 13, 1997 and never received any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill targeted companies that treat workers as independent contractors when those workers really function as employees, a practice that lets employers skip payroll taxes and benefits. It would have narrowed the legal "safe harbor" that shields employers from back employment taxes (allowing that defense only after a recent IRS audit confirmed the classification), repealed special treatment for skilled technical personnel, and required employers to warn workers on tax statements that being classified as a contractor means no employee benefits and possible loss of legal protections. It would also have set a single federal definition of "employee" for unemployment compensation, extending coverage to misclassified workers. The bill never received a vote. [S2, S3, S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who are treated as independent contractors but function as employees would gain: employers would have to tell them on payment statements that they may owe self-employment tax, are losing fringe benefits, and are not covered by wage, safety, civil rights, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation laws, along with how to ask the IRS to review their status. A uniform federal definition of "employee" would also extend unemployment compensation coverage to misclassified workers. [S2, S3]

how_it_helps.text: Workers misclassified as independent contractors would, for the first time, be told in writing on payment statements that they may owe self-employment tax, get no fringe benefits, and may lose protections under wage, safety, civil rights, unemployment insurance, and workers' compensation laws — plus how to ask the IRS to review their status.

The bill would close a major loophole: today an employer can avoid back employment taxes by showing any 'reasonable basis' for treating a worker as a contractor; the bill would allow that defense only if a recent IRS employment tax audit specifically approved the classification.

It would repeal the blanket exemption for skilled technical personnel and restore the IRS's authority to issue regulations and rulings on employment status, giving workers a clearer path to challenge their classification.
It would set one federal definition of 'employee' that states must use for unemployment compensation, so workers misclassified as contractors could not be shut out of unemployment benefits.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that use independent contractors would pay employment taxes on reclassified workers, would lose the ability to rely on a vague "reasonable basis" defense (only a recent IRS audit would count), would have to sign closing agreements subject to five years of Treasury monitoring, and would have to add new warnings to 1099-type statements. Businesses misclassifying in good faith could wipe out past tax liability only by agreeing to treat such workers as employees going forward. [S2, S3]

drawbacks.text: The new safe harbor would let employers who misclassified workers escape back employment taxes, penalties, and interest entirely — provided they claim good faith, file consistently, and sign a closing agreement — a real revenue loss to the Treasury and a windfall for past nonpayment.

Allowing a 'reasonable basis' defense only after a recent, qualifying IRS audit could be costly and burdensome for small businesses, effectively requiring a paid audit to be certain of any contractor classification.
The added notice requirements on 1099-type statements would impose new paperwork on every business that pays independent contractors, even those with legitimate classifications.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's main effect runs clearly in workers' favor: it narrows a loophole that lets employers avoid payroll taxes and benefits, extends unemployment coverage, and forces disclosure to workers of what contractor status costs them. The trade-off is real but narrower: employers who misclassified in good faith get a clean slate on back taxes if they reclassify going forward, and all businesses paying contractors face new notice paperwork and, effectively, a need for IRS audits to be safe. The audit-only standard is aggressive, but the bill pairs it with a clear amnesty path, which softens the burden. On balance the costs fall mostly on the businesses whose practice the bill exists to stop.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and never came up for a vote.

narrative.text: Representative Tom Lantos introduced the bill on February 13, 1997, joined by Representative Christopher Shays and one other Republican cosponsor.
The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day of introduction and never moved.
Lantos delivered introductory remarks in the Congressional Record on March 6, 1997, the only other recorded action.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that classify workers as independent contractors are better off, because the crackdown never happened: they continue to avoid employment taxes, and misclassified workers continue to go without employee benefits and unemployment insurance coverage.

for.name: Tom Lantos
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Misclassification of Employees Act on February 13, 1997.

for.name: Christopher Shays
for.what_they_did: Joined as the named original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

for.name: One additional House Republican cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only recorded support in the chamber besides the sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: House committee with jurisdiction over tax law
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearings, no markup, no report — so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded support was the Democratic sponsor and two Republican cosponsors; no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.industry: Businesses that rely on independent contractors
industries.note: The bill's core provisions strike at the main financial advantage of treating workers as contractors: escaping employment taxes, benefits, and unemployment insurance contributions. Only a recent IRS audit would support the classification, and new warnings to workers would make reclassification challenges easier.
Firms supplying technical personnel would lose the section 530(d) exemption that currently shields their contractor classifications from IRS challenge.
Misclassified workers do not pay into state unemployment systems or draw from them when out of work; a uniform federal definition of employee would bring them into the system's tax and benefit base.
